title: The Trans Aseer Mountain Range: A Hidden World in the Peninsula – Abe Alkhamees
content:
This is a firsthand account of the first stage of the Trans Aseer Route, a 1,100-mile bikepacking route across the fog-wrapped ridges of Saudi Arabia’s Aseer Mountains from Jeddah to Jazan. It covers dead-end roads, baboon-raided campsites, endless cups of tea, and a journey back to author and route designer Abe Alkhamees’ ancestral roots. Will you join Stage One in January 2027?

The wind rumbles up from a precipitous void, rising from the vast lowland expanse of the Tahama, thousands of feet below. Off my right shoulder, the sun remains hidden behind a shifting wall of clouds while the mountain fog rolls across the ridge ahead in rhythmic, chilly waves. The fog offers no middle ground when it shows up, layer up or shiver away. You put on an extra layer to cut the dampness and cold, only for the sun to suddenly tear open a moment later, releasing a searing heat that bakes the moisture right off of you while you scramble to strip that jacket back off before you boil.

The sheer verticality of these mountains does not accommodate sitting and spinning a light gear, my 34×51 could barely keep up anyways… My legs and lungs were entirely spent, and a few bike lengths ahead, Ali kept his head down, both of us rightfully cooked. The rocky tracks just kept climbing higher into the clouds with no end in sight.

What the hell are we even doing out here?

On paper, neither Ali nor I had any logical business loving mountains this much. We grew up only three hours apart from each other, him in Saudi Arabia and me in Kuwait, raised on the same flat, coastal topography where the horizon stretches for miles without a single hill to break up the sky. Yet we originally crossed paths thousands of miles away on a bike ride in Oregon, the place where my relationship with this type of “fun” originally took root. Now, years later, we were orbiting Planet Bonk on Stage One of a route that had consumed five years of my life to map and build.

The Acclimation

Our trip had begun at 8:00 am at 6500ft, assembling the loaded rigs and packing a few local provisions for the high passes. We fueled ourselves on Ma’soub, a dense, traditional bowl of heavy bread pudding laced with honey, bananas, nuts, and cream. It sits on the absolute opposite end of modern sports nutrition, but it provides the exact kind of slow-burning caloric density required to survive the steep gradients ahead. Starting at that elevation left my head buzzing from the thin air, but the elation of the journey ahead was the best cure for this oxygen hangover.

The route immediately dropped from the cool ridge of Al Hada down a long, serpentine paved ribbon that snaked toward the high desert of Taif, the mountain scrub quickly falling away as the road shimmered into the deep red valley below.

The pavement ended where the double tracks picked up, just past a farmer in the terraces with a confused look on his face, probably wondering if we were lost. The tracks climbed straight up, and over a giant rocky hill we’d been staring at since morning, loose chunder and pockets of sand the whole way through the Wadi. We rode for hours through one valley after another, the mountains slowly closing in on both sides toward a watershed system. Even knowing the route by heart, for a moment it looked like there wasn’t a way through, until the gravel line came into view, scaling straight up the mountainside, and we followed it until it broke into a pass, with AlShafa Mountains just around the corner.

Evening fog rolled in from a distance, rising from the Tahama, and cast its darkness over everything it touched, turning day into temporary night, as if we’d rolled into another realm entirely. It shrouded us briefly, then let go. We came out the other side back to civilization as if we hadn’t just spent the last stretch pushing bikes up a seemingly dead-end valley.

Wadi Bani Sa’ad

In Arabic, Aseer translates to harsh or difficult, which is the exact reality of this terrain, and these mountains live up to their name in every mile, thin air, steep grades, rugged terrain, pushing a fully loaded bike up yet another pass. Five years of scouting this mountain range and I still end up walking half of those passes more than pedaling them.

I keep coming back anyway.

In 2021, after my US visa renewal was rejected and I was forced to leave the Pacific Northwest after 9 years, my body gave up trying to carry the stress my spirit was still fighting against. Looking for an anchor, I began digging into family history, chasing lore that eventually led me straight back to this northern section of the range. This unassuming valley of Bani Sa’ad is the furthest back we can trace our own lineage, roughly 1,500 years.

None of it prepared us for actually rolling in on a loaded bike, legs still wrecked from the climb, looking at the same stone those maps only ever showed me from above. Arriving here after everything these first few days had put us through humbled me, experiencing the origins of where my family comes from, and how far they traveled for hundreds of years.

That night the wind was pushing us sideways, so we sheltered near some old growth juniper. Tired as we were, none of it mattered next to the sights and the people we’d met along the way, every interaction filling our cups, sometimes with words of encouragement and prayers, most times just tea. We slept under an open sky once the fog cleared up, only to wak up at dawn to find the entire campsite soaked through by the dense morning mist. Our gear was scattered across the dirt, the local baboons having raided our packs while we slept, a backcountry variable we forgot to prepare for that night

The Dead End

I’ve lost count of the days at that point. Ali and I are still in awe of what we kept experiencing throughout the journey so far. The small conversations with people along the way, and the mid-day break at a mosque in a tiny village, all of that deepened an already rich experience.

Past the giant lantern along a main road, we turned towards the mountains before a local stopped us in our tracks. “Asalam Alikom! You know this road is closed, right? It’s a dead end; it doesn’t go anywhere.” Concerned with this news from the locals, I hesitantly replied, “We’re going to the village on the ridge up there,” as I pointed to it high above the ridge. His face dropped. “How did you even know about that?!” With a mix of optimism, knowledge, and purely winging it, we regained confidence and flew down the valley for some time before the grueling 27% grade went up towards a large “END OF ROAD” sign.

Past the sign, and across the village was a sandy climb scaling the peak, taking us back up the ridge again as the sun was sinking below towards the Tahama.

A daily ritual at this point.

The Sarawat

By now we were deep in the Sarawat (highlands), juniper trees were dense on both sides of the road and the air was noticeably cooler, especially when the fog rose up from the valleys, as it usually does, almost on the clock. It’s like stepping into a walk-in fridge on a hot summer day in the middle of a ride. It’s one of the closest things I experienced to feeling time itself slow down. Traffic fades, birds find their roost, and silence reigns supreme.

Well… except for our shoes over the chunky gravel climb, on the edge of the ridge.

What the hell are we even doing out here again? It’s only a short-lived sentiment when you move through the Trans Aseer Mountain Range route.

For me, this geography has become a never-ending journey, and I prefer it that way. Tracing this route out of my own family lore sparked a project that eventually grew into something much larger than just an idea. My connection to these mountains runs deeper than the surface appeal of a dramatic landscape. My hope is that by venturing into these high passes, riding where people lived, traveled, and survived for generations, some of that shared history finds you too, in this expansive and still unexplored part of the world.

The Route

The full route spans 1100 miles from Jeddah to Jazan and packs well over 100k ft of elevation. In Arabic, Aseer translates to harsh or difficult, which is the exact reality of this terrain. The line immediately leaves the coast to hold a sustained average elevation of 6500 feet, topping out just shy of 10,000ft atop Jabal Sawda. It is a slow, heavy grind across a mix of gravel roads, loose wadi chunder, and primitive dirt tracks.

The geography shifts completely across three distinct chapters. It begins with the exposed plains of the High Desert, climbs into the cold mist and dense juniper forests of the central Sarawat, and finishes among the radically steep stone terraces of the southern Coffee Belt.

Want to ride Stage One?

If this has inspired you and you’re the type of bikepacker that appreciates the blend of history, connection with the land, and an unforgettable journey, then Stage One might be a good trip to mark on your January calendar. I’ll be hosting a shortlist of riders from all over the world to join the ride in January 2027 to ride Stage One, roughly 350 miles of uncompromising terrain, packing 40,000 feet of climbing and topping out at 8,800 feet of altitude, across this hidden world.
